Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: Has the world really overcome its divisions? Source : Lilian Afreh-Sika Boateng 10 November 2026 5:24am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
On 9 November 1989, the world witnessed one of the most remarkable turning points in modern political history. In Berlin, Germany, thousands gathered at border crossings, embraced strangers, reunited with family members, and began dismantling a concrete structure that had separated communities for almost three decades. The Berlin Wall, once a powerful symbol of political division and ideological rivalry, was finally breached.
Thirty-seven years later, this historic event remains relevant, not merely as a chapter in European history but as an important lesson in international relations, diplomacy, democracy, sovereignty and the changing global order.
But to appreciate the significance of that night, we must first understand why the Wall was built.
At the end of the Second World War in 1945, Germany was defeated and divided into four occupation zones administered by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union.
As political and ideological tensions between the Western powers and the Soviet Union intensified, the country eventually developed into two separate states.
West Germany, officially the Federal Republic of Germany, embraced a democratic political system and a market-oriented economy and maintained close ties with Western Europe and the United States.
East Germany, officially the German Democratic Republic, adopted a socialist political and economic system under Soviet influence.
Even Berlin, although situated within East Germany, was divided into eastern and western sectors.
The division represented more than territorial boundaries. It reflected the ideological confrontation between capitalism and communism, democracy and authoritarianism, and two competing visions of how societies should be governed.
In August 1961, East German authorities began constructing the Berlin Wall to prevent citizens from fleeing to West Berlin. What started as a heavily guarded barrier became a complex border system of concrete walls, watchtowers, fences, and security installations.
For 28 years, the Wall separated families, restricted freedom of movement and became one of the most recognisable symbols of the Cold War.
The fall of the Berlin Wall was not an isolated incident or simply the result of one political announcement. It culminated years of political dissatisfaction, economic hardship, civil resistance, and changing international circumstances.
Across Eastern Europe, citizens were increasingly demanding political reforms and greater freedoms.
In Poland, the Solidarity movement challenged communist rule. Hungary began dismantling its border restrictions with Austria, creating opportunities for East Germans to travel westward. Meanwhile, mass demonstrations in East Germany intensified pressure on the government.
The Soviet Union, under Mikhail Gorbachev, had also introduced political and economic reforms, signalling a departure from the previous approach of using military intervention to maintain communist governments in Eastern Europe.
During a press conference, East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel regulations. When asked when the new arrangements would take effect, he said they applied immediately, though the situation was more complicated than his announcement suggested.
Thousands of East Germans rushed to the border crossings. Faced with mounting crowds and lacking clear instructions, border officials eventually opened the gates.
People crossed freely for the first time in decades. Celebrations erupted, and citizens began breaking pieces off the Wall.
It demonstrated how political systems that appear permanent can be transformed by a combination of public determination, political change, and international circumstances.
This distinction is important and often overlooked in public discussion.
The fall of the Berlin Wall accelerated the decline of the Cold War order, but it did not formally mark the end of the Cold War.
Germany officially reunified on 3 October 1990, after negotiations among the two German states and the four former occupying powers.
The Soviet Union itself dissolved in December 1991, marking another major turning point in international politics.
The collapse of the Soviet Union effectively ended the bipolar international system that had dominated global politics for decades.
The United States emerged as the world’s predominant global power, while European countries pursued deeper political and economic integration.
However, the end of the Cold War did not eliminate geopolitical rivalry. Instead, the international system continued to evolve, producing new security challenges, competing interests and emerging centres of global influence.
Today, renewed tensions among major powers, the war in Ukraine, strategic competition between the United States and China, and the growing influence of emerging economies demonstrate that international politics remains dynamic.
The world did not become free of divisions simply because one wall came down.
For Africa, the anniversary offers an opportunity to reflect on our own historical and contemporary divisions.
Unlike Germany, Africa’s fragmentation is not primarily the result of a single ideological confrontation. It is rooted in a complex history of colonial boundaries, political differences, weak regional infrastructure, trade restrictions, economic fragmentation and institutional challenges.
The continent comprises 55 African Union member states, many of which still face barriers to cross-border trade and economic cooperation.
Despite its enormous natural resources, youthful population, and significant productive potential, intra-African trade remains relatively low compared with other major trading regions.
This is where the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) becomes particularly important.
AfCFTA is not a political reunification project. It does not seek to abolish national sovereignty or merge African countries into one state. Instead, it aims to create a single continental market for goods and services, strengthen regional value chains, facilitate investment, and promote economic cooperation.
Its ambition is to move Africa beyond the limitations of fragmented national markets toward a more competitive, integrated continental economy.
The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) is another important development. By facilitating cross-border payments in African local currencies, PAPSS seeks to reduce dependence on third-party currencies and make intra-African trade more efficient.
However, integration requires more than signing agreements and establishing institutions. It demands political commitment, effective implementation, infrastructure development, financial cooperation and the removal of non-tariff barriers.
German reunification reminds us that overcoming division requires deliberate institutional and political action. It also reminds us that integration brings economic, social, and administrative challenges that cannot be ignored.
Africa must therefore pursue integration not merely as a political aspiration but as a practical economic development strategy.
Thirty-seven years after the fall of the Berlin Wall, we must confront an uncomfortable question: have we genuinely built a more united world, or have the walls simply taken different forms?
Some barriers are no longer made of concrete. They exist in restrictive immigration policies, trade protectionism, financial exclusion, geopolitical competition, technological inequalities and unequal access to economic opportunities.
Countries may maintain diplomatic relations while pursuing policies that undermine international cooperation.
Globalisation has connected markets, but it has not necessarily eliminated inequality. International institutions have expanded, but questions about representation, fairness and the distribution of global power remain unresolved.
For Africa, this raises an important question about our place in the emerging international order. We cannot continue to advocate for a borderless economic future while maintaining unnecessary barriers to trade, investment, movement and regional cooperation among ourselves.
The lesson of 9 November 1989 is not simply that walls can fall. Political realities are not permanent, and determined populations, changing leadership, and diplomatic engagement can reshape the course of history.
The Berlin Wall separated people physically, politically and economically. Its fall created an opportunity for a different future, although that future required years of difficult negotiations, institutional adjustments and national reconciliation.
As Africans, our challenge is to build a continent where borders facilitate cooperation rather than obstruct opportunity; where economic integration translates into jobs and prosperity; and where our collective voice carries greater weight in global affairs.
Perhaps the greatest lesson from the fall of the Berlin Wall is that the future belongs not to those who build the strongest barriers, but to those with the courage, vision, and political will to dismantle them.
Thirty-seven years later, the question remains: what walls must Africa dismantle to realise the promise of Agenda 2063?
The writer, Lilian Afreh-Sika Boateng, is a Certified Economic and Trade Diplomat, Certified AfCFTA Professional
